services.d: Welcome, browse abandon, cart recovery, post-purchase, winback and replenishment — built once, earning daily.
A calendar that ships on time, with copy, design and segmentation handled end to end.
Table-based templates that survive Outlook, respect dark mode, and load on a slow connection.
Subject lines, preview text and body copy written for one reader, not a demographic.
Behaviour, value and recency segments that stop you sending the same email to everybody.
Authentication, warm-up, list hygiene and re-engagement so what you send reaches the inbox.
The channel mix, cadence and offer architecture behind repeat purchase.

process.d: We audit your account, flows, list health and last ninety days of sends, then interview the people who talk to your customers.
A lifecycle map: which flows exist, which are missing, what each one is worth, and the order we build them in.
Copy, design and build. Every email is written for a specific moment in the customer relationship, not a template slot.
Staged rollout with deliverability monitoring, so volume ramps without putting your sending reputation at risk.
Subject lines, offers, timing and segments tested against revenue per recipient — never against opens alone.
Monthly reporting, a rolling campaign calendar, and new flows as the catalogue and customer base change.

faqs.q: How long before we see anything?
faqs.a: The audit lands in week one and the first rebuilt flow is usually live by week two. Compounding revenue from the full lifecycle takes a quarter — anyone promising faster is selling you a discount code.

faqs.q: Which email platforms do you work in?
faqs.a: Klaviyo most often, then Mailchimp, Omnisend and Customer.io. If your stack is something else, say so on the call and we will tell you honestly whether we are the right people.

faqs.q: Who owns the flows you build?
faqs.a: You do. Everything is built inside your own account, documented, and yours to keep whether we work together for three months or three years.
Three months, because retention work genuinely does not show its full shape faster than that. After the first three it runs month to month.

faqs.q: Our list is small. Are we too early?
faqs.a: Possibly, and we will say so. Below a few thousand engaged subscribers your money is usually better spent on acquisition first. We would rather tell you that than take the retainer.

cases.title: Campaigns and flows that grew the email revenue
cases.overview: A four-year-old wellness brand with 63,000 subscribers, one welcome email and a monthly newsletter. Everything else was paid acquisition.
cases.challenge: Rising CAC had squeezed margin to the point where growth was costing more than it returned. The list was the largest untouched asset in the business, and nobody owned it.
cases.strategy: We rebuilt the lifecycle from zero: a five-part welcome series segmented by skin concern, browse and cart recovery, a post-purchase education track, and a replenishment trigger tied to product size. Copy was rewritten around the barrier-first philosophy the founder actually talks about.

cases.title: Recovering the checkout, without discounting it
cases.overview: A technical apparel brand losing four in five carts and papering over it with a standing 15% recovery code.
cases.challenge: The discount had trained customers to abandon deliberately. Recovery revenue looked healthy while average order value quietly fell for three straight quarters.
cases.strategy: We killed the automatic code and replaced it with objection handling — sizing, returns, durability — in a three-email sequence timed to one hour, one day and three days. The discount survives only in the final email, and only for first-time buyers.

cases.title: A launch that sold out before the ads went live
cases.overview: An eighteen-month product development cycle with one shot at a launch, and a list that had never been segmented.
cases.challenge: Sending one announcement to everybody would have burned the most engaged buyers on a generic email and buried the rest in an inbox they never open.
cases.strategy: Three waves. Waitlist first with founder-written context and no discount, then recent browsers with a comparison against the old product, then the full list with social proof from the first 48 hours. Suppression rules stopped anyone receiving two.

cases.title: Waking over 38,000 subscribers who had stopped listening
cases.overview: Half the list had not opened an email in over a year, and it was dragging deliverability down for the half that had.
cases.challenge: Sending more to a dormant list was making things worse. Inbox placement had slipped far enough that even engaged subscribers were landing in Promotions.
cases.strategy: Authentication and list hygiene first, then a three-email winback at day 180 with a genuine reason to return rather than a coupon. Anyone still silent moved to a sunset path and off the active list entirely.

cases.title: Remove the Final Friction
cases.overview: A strategic, automated abandoned cart email sequence designed to recover high intent lost revenue.
cases.challenge: Missed Revenue: Valuable traffic and ad spend were being wasted because there was no automated safety net to bring interested buyers back.
cases.strategy: Friction Removal & Reassurance: Instead of just showing the item, we proactively addressed common drop-off barriers (like shipping concerns, security trust badges, and FAQs) directly inside the email layout.
